progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c03 (net ionic reaction, ΔH negative for a rise, enthalpy of neutralisation per mole of water, about −57 kJ/mol for fully ionised pairs, q = mcΔT with the total mass, n = cV, ΔH = −q ÷ n(H₂O), rounding to the data's significant figures, heat loss named as the likely reason a result is less negative). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability and accuracy in plain words; risk assessment as hazard, harm, control; independent, dependent and controlled variables). Year 11 Module 4 (calorimetry, specific heat capacity). Year 11 Working Scientifically (drawing a line of best fit).
progression.startsWith: Set up an insulated calorimeter and record starting conditions. The video opens: Here's an odd thing about this experiment. When you mix an acid and a base in a foam cup, the thermometer doesn't show the highest temperature the mixture could reach. Heat starts escaping the moment it's made, so by the time the reading peaks, some is already gone.
progression.stopsAfter: setting up an insulated, lidded, supported cup and explaining each part; measuring and averaging both starting temperatures; logging past the peak; plotting the temperature-time graph and extrapolating the cooling line to the mixing time, with its assumption; calculating ΔH from the extrapolated rise; naming the controlled variables of a repeated measurement; tracing an error through ΔT, q and ΔH; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk rows for 1.00 mol/L NaOH and HCl. No weak acids (chem-m6-c09), no applications (chem-m6-c04), no percentage uncertainty.
progression.nextLesson: where neutralisation solves a real problem (route chem-m6-c04).

teaching.task: The thermometer never catches the full temperature rise, because heat escapes from the moment it is made. So how do you set up the enthalpy of neutralisation experiment, and how do you recover the temperature you never see?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) heat escapes from the moment it is made, so the highest reading is too low (1); (2) foam traps air and conducts little heat; the lid cuts the heat carried away by warm air and vapour; the beaker stops tipping; measured volumes set both the moles and the mass (2); (3) a warmer solution would raise the reading without any reaction, so both starting temperatures are measured and averaged (3); (4) the readings after the peak are needed for the cooling line (4); (5) the cup loses heat during the rise as well, so the peak is lower than the no-loss temperature (5); (6) the reaction itself is almost instant, so with no loss the temperature would jump at the moment of mixing; extending the straight cooling line back to that time estimates the no-loss temperature, assuming the same cooling rate (6); (7) the C03 calculation with the extrapolated rise gives a value closer to −57 than the highest reading does (7); (8) a repeated measurement has controlled variables but no deliberately changed variable between runs (8); (9) each error traced through ΔT, q and ΔH; heat loss and heat absorbed by the cup and probe push ΔH less negative, but a starting temperature recorded too low pushes it more negative; name the cause (9); (10) validity, reliability, accuracy; repeats cannot fix heat loss, because it lowers every run (10); (11) the real hazards and their controls (11); memory aid (12); attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the thermometer never shows the temperature the mixture could reach, because heat escapes from the moment it is made, and the practical is built around recovering that hidden peak. Each part of the set-up is given its reason (a foam cup in a beaker, a lid, measured volumes), both starting temperatures are measured and averaged, readings are logged every 30 seconds well past the peak, and the cooling line on the temperature-time graph is extended back to the moment of mixing because the reaction itself is almost instant. The C03 calculation is staged one line at a time with the extrapolated rise; the variables of a repeated measurement, each error traced through delta T, q and delta H, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment follow. The memory aid "Lid on. Log on. Line back." closes the method. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's an odd thing about this experiment. When you mix an acid and a base in a foam cup, the thermometer doesn't show the highest temperature the mixture could reach. Heat starts escaping the moment it's made, so by the time the reading peaks, some is already gone. That's partly why the last video's answer fell short of minus fifty seven. So how do you set it up, and how do you measure a temperature you never actually see?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "50.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L nitric acid and 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L potassium hydroxide solution, both at 20.9 °C, are mixed in a lidded polystyrene cup at time 0. The temperature is recorded every 30 seconds, as shown in the graph. Assume the density of the mixture is 1.00 g/mL and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Use the graph to determine the temperature change, then calculate the molar enthalpy of neutralisation." New acid and base, new numbers, the viewer must extrapolate. Answer −54 kJ/mol. Crossed mistake: the highest reading, 27.1 °C, giving −52 kJ/mol. (A2) "A student mixes 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L hydrochloric acid with 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution in an uncovered glass beaker. She records the highest temperature shown on a thermometer and calculates the enthalpy of neutralisation as −46 kJ/mol. Identify the main source of error in her method, explain its effect on the calculated value, and suggest one improvement." Answer: heat loss through the glass and open top; ΔT, q too small; ΔH less negative; lidded foam cup and extrapolation. Crossed mistake: "human error".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation (ACSCH093)" this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the calorimetry practical; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: the insulated, lidded, supported cup and why each part is there; measuring both starting temperatures and averaging them; logging temperature at intervals past the peak; the temperature-time graph; extrapolating the cooling line back to the moment of mixing, and its assumption; the error chain (source, then ΔT, then q, then ΔH); the controlled variables of a repeated measurement; validity, reliability and accuracy for this practical; the risk assessment. Not re-taught: why neutralisation releases heat, the sign of ΔH, the per-mole-of-water definition, q = mcΔT with the total mass, moles of water from the reactant that runs out (all chem-m6-c03; scene 7 runs the C03 method in one compact pass, one stage per line, saying "as in the last video"). Not here: weak acids and why their values differ (chem-m6-c09; the site's L10 strong-against-weak comparison is not used); applications (chem-m6-c04); Hess's law; percentage uncertainty arithmetic. Validity, reliability and accuracy were given plain meanings in chem-m5-p01; scene 10 recalls them in one clause each and applies them here.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C03): H⁺ teal, OH⁻ violet (only if a lens is used; none is planned); heat warm orange arrows; the temperature readout amber digits; graph points amber, the cooling line teal, the extrapolation dashed teal; hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus or the graph; the right third holds the current card (method step, working, error chain, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends.
